medical.title: Study will test whether hyperbaric oxygen therapy can ease invisible brain injuries in veterans
medical.summary: When veterans walk through the doors of USF Health's Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT) Center, they often carry wounds that are not visible.

medical.title: Could the way we walk give clues about our mental health?
medical.summary: Experts in kinesiology and sport sciences and psychology from the University of Miami are collaborating on research to find out whether the way people walk could give clues about their mental health. The two researchers are exploring this question through a project called MindStep, where participants answer survey questions about their mental health and then complete different intellectual tasks while walking, as specialized cameras record and measure their walking patterns.

medical.title: Scientists turn protein-making errors in cancer cells into a targeted kill switch
medical.summary: Like every other cell in the human body, cancer cells also produce their own share of proteins for survival. During this production process, cells often encounter a glitch called ribosomal frameshifting. This exceptionally rare event occurs roughly once in every 100,000 translation events, when the ribosome, while reading genetic instructions to make a protein, shifts its reading position. A recent Nature study investigated whether this protein-building glitch in cancer cells can be turned into a targeted cancer therapy.

medical.title: The brain's 'dimmer switch' could help explain why attention drifts
medical.summary: McGill researchers have discovered that serotonin, a brain chemical best known for its role in mood and mental health, also helps regulate attention. "Our findings suggest serotonin-producing neurons deep in the midbrain act like a dimmer switch on attention," said Arjun Krishnaswamy, associate professor in the Department of Physiology, who co-led the study with associate professor Erik Cook. The findings were published in Nature Communications.

medical.title: Organizations call for rapid, team-based endovascular hemorrhage control in trauma care
medical.summary: The American College of Surgeons (ACS) Committee on Trauma and the Society of Interventional Radiology (SIR) have issued a joint position statement reaffirming the role of interventional radiologists on multidisciplinary trauma teams and the importance of establishing reliable systems for rapid endovascular hemorrhage control in trauma situations.

medical.title: AI assesses what really matters to people in health care—well-being
medical.summary: Artificial intelligence is helping to analyze and improve health care systems—from waiting times to treatment outcomes and costs. However, some of the most important aspects of care remain harder to measure—such as whether people feel heard, understood and genuinely cared for.

medical.title: Early trial results suggest potential new treatment for stiff person syndrome
medical.summary: A multicenter clinical trial evaluating chimeric antigen receptor-T cell therapy (CAR-T cell therapy) for stiff person syndrome (SPS), a rare autoimmune neurologic disorder, has produced promising early results.

medical.title: US youths see nearly 4,000 food marketing messages on digital media each year
medical.summary: U.S. children and adolescents see thousands of food marketing messages on digital media platforms each year, according to new research published in JAMA Pediatrics. And 92% of the marketed food and beverage products are considered unhealthy.

medical.title: It takes a neighborhood to keep kids active
medical.summary: Getting youngsters to go outside and play doesn't just rely on family support, but also on a neighborhood coming together to create a good environment, University of Alberta research shows.

medical.title: Two-year study will examine how gender-affirming hormone therapy affects energy use and blood vessel function
medical.summary: The research team at the LeiCeM Cluster of Excellence is preparing a new study. It builds on the first phase of the Hormones and Health study (HHS), in which researchers from the Helmholtz Institute for Metabolic, Obesity and Vascular Research (HI-MAG), Leipzig University and the University of Leipzig Medical Center followed trans people undergoing gender-affirming hormone therapy. The second cohort will be studied over a period of two years, with the study expected to begin in early 2027.

medical.title: Study challenges long-held fears about overactive bladder drugs and dementia
medical.summary: New research published in JAMA Network Open finds anticholinergic medications, commonly prescribed for overactive bladder (OAB), may not increase dementia risk after all compared to beta-3 agonists, the newer drug class that has been presumed to be safer for the brain.

medical.title: Why obesity affects males and females differently
medical.summary: University of California, Riverside, scientists have an explanation for why males and females respond differently to obesity. They report in PNAS Nexus that certain immune cell populations in fat tissue may protect against obesity-related inflammation while others may contribute to harmful metabolic changes. They found these immune cells, called eosinophils and traditionally associated with asthma and allergies, behave differently in males and females.

medical.title: Your brain may map emotional concepts onto a hexagonal grid, new study suggests
medical.summary: Everyday life throws a whole range of emotional experiences our way, from exciting and relaxing moments to tense or gloomy encounters. Each experience is shaped by what's present around us in the moment, the sensations our body is experiencing and our past experiences. This entire scene is set by the brain, which draws on these experiences of the past, organizing the information it gathers into mental maps that help us predict what might happen and respond appropriately to different situations.

medical.title: In phase 2 trial, novel therapy significantly reduced triglyceride levels
medical.summary: A phase 2b clinical trial led by Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute researchers shows that a monoclonal antibody therapy called MAR001 can significantly reduce triglyceride levels within 12 weeks for patients with high triglyceride levels. Their results are published in the New England Journal of Medicine and were presented simultaneously at the American Heart Association's annual meeting.

medical.title: Childhood cancers may spread by 'shape-shifting' rather than mutating
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of East Anglia (UK) have proposed an explanation for why some childhood tumors spread aggressively around the body despite having relatively few genetic faults. For years, experts believed cancers become more dangerous by accumulating genetic mutations that allow them to invade new tissues and evade treatment. But a new paper shows how childhood cancers may not always need extra mutations to spread.

medical.title: ‘Digital advances are reshaping nature conservation’ say experts
medical.summary: Technology and the rapid advance of AI are opening up new possibilities in the race to save nature, according to a report The post ‘Digital advances are reshaping nature conservation’ say experts appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: Magnetic fields can revive intracellular transport in ALS
medical.summary: A study led by cell biologist Dr. Arun Pal at the HZDR, in collaboration with research partners in Dresden and Rostock, has found that electromagnetic alternating fields can partially reverse key pathological changes in human nerve cells. The finding has been published in the journal Cells.

medical.title: Cleaner bedroom air may help manage blood sugar in prediabetes
medical.summary: Using portable filters to reduce exposure to air pollution during sleep may stabilize the large spikes in blood sugar experienced by people with prediabetes, a condition in which sugar (glucose) levels are higher than normal, a new study shows.

medical.title: Concussion study upends understanding of what makes head impacts dangerous
medical.summary: Concussions—essentially mild traumatic brain injuries—are among the most common injuries sustained on athletic fields. In the U.S., an estimated 3.8 million sports-related concussions occur every year. But new research by Stanford Medicine scientists and collaborators suggests that the prevailing understanding of the forces that lead to concussion may be missing the mark.

medical.title: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered that pantethine, a readily available vitamin B5 derivative, can calm overactive immune cells and may help fight psoriasis. The supplement prevented psoriasis in mice and showed promising results in a small human trial, revealing an unexpected connection between cholesterol and autoimmune inflammation.

medical.title: A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer
medical.summary: A surprising new study from UCLA suggests that a naturally occurring molecule could help breast cancer survivors overcome the frustrating brain fog and exhaustion that can linger long after treatment ends. Researchers found that women taking an oxaloacetate supplement for eight weeks experienced substantial improvements in memory, concentration, mental clarity, and fatigue.

medical.title: AI predicts PTSD risk based on stories about what brought patients to the emergency room
medical.summary: An AI tool can analyze patients' narratives about injuries that sent them to the emergency room to predict who will later develop posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a new study found.

medical.title: Could a plant metabolite act as a natural sunscreen to help prevent skin cancer?
medical.summary: Research in Photochemistry and Photobiology indicates that a plant metabolite that can block the effects of ultraviolet (UV) light has promising potential as a natural sunscreen when applied to human skin.

medical.title: Cancer clinical trial participants reimbursed a median $2,128 for nonmedical expenses
medical.summary: New research reveals that participating in cancer clinical trials can cause financial burdens that are shaped by both socioeconomic and logistical factors. The analysis published by Wiley online in CANCER, indicates the need for better reimbursement programs to improve equitable access to, and retention in, cancer clinical trials.

medical.title: What went right this week: the good news that matters
medical.summary: Nature was restored at ‘unprecedented scale’, Barbados halted HIV transmission in babies, and a fuel revolution picked up speed, plus more The post What went right this week: the good news that matters appeared first on Positive News .

science.title: Two nearby rocky worlds could offer alien astronomers views of planets appearing to reverse course
science.summary: Aliens have long been a staple of science fiction. Yet the possibility of intelligent life beyond Earth is more than a matter of imagination—it is also a subject of serious scientific inquiry. Professor Woong-bae Zee of Sejong University's School of Liberal Studies has recently published an astronomy paper that places the word "alien" front and center.

science.title: The fastest levitated spinning magnet ever made might help physicists search for dark matter
science.summary: Tiny levitated magnets are able to avoid contact friction, making them useful for detecting extremely weak forces and magnetic fields and acting as ultralow-noise quantum sensors and precision measurement tools. Combining levitation with extreme cold further reduces unwanted motion that can make faint signals hard to detect.

science.title: Satellite monitoring of the world's oceans is being restricted by legal barriers, study suggests
science.summary: Satellite technology can increasingly track vessels across the world's oceans and has the ability to detect industrial fishing inside marine protected areas (MPAs). But new research has suggested that regulations governing these often vulnerable parts of our planet could be preventing global authorities from turning satellite detection into effective enforcement.

science.title: Repeated racism linked to depression and suicidal thoughts in Colorado teens
science.summary: Knowing that multiple studies provide strong evidence that links racism to poor mental health, researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz wanted to know what types of racist incidents young people are experiencing in schools and if repeated events were more harmful to their mental health.

science.title: The art of good conversation may involve a little pink noise
science.summary: Most of us like a good old chat with friends, colleagues, neighbors or acquaintances. But what can turn a really good chat into a great one? Sure, conversation topics matter, but scientists have found underlying patterns that may explain our best interactions.

science.title: Prehistoric whale reveals extreme skull asymmetry
science.summary: Sperm whales and pygmy sperm whales are known among mammals for their unusually shaped heads. Unlike most vertebrates, which are bilaterally symmetrical, toothed whales have asymmetrical skulls that accommodate highly specialized organs used for echolocation and sound production.

science.title: Smart use of trees and crops brings best yield
science.summary: Cultivating crops—such as wheat, barley and rye—alongside rows of trees is a system of agroforestry that is known as "alley-cropping." It serves many functions: in addition to enhancing ecosystems and biodiversity, it can also counteract the negative effects of growing crops in treeless open land. The advantages of alley-cropping come from the interaction between trees and crops, resulting in improved soil quality, reduced wind erosion, enhanced nutrient cycling, and climate change mitigation through increased carbon capture.

science.title: 'Nice' by any other name means essentially the same thing
science.summary: Is any good deed truly selfless—and does it matter?

science.title: Cells 'sense' physical forces to seal tissues and protect organs
science.summary: Northwestern Medicine scientists have uncovered a molecular mechanism that enables cells to protect organs from leaks, infection and inflammation, according to a study published in the Journal of Cell Biology. The findings of the study add to scientific understanding of how epithelial cells maintain protective barriers, said senior author Cara J. Gottardi, professor of medicine in the Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care and of cell and developmental biology.

science.title: Why demand persists for the horn of a once near-extinct antelope
science.summary: Family traditions, misconceptions about where it comes from, and a belief that remedies sold in shops are government-approved help explain continued demand for saiga antelope horn in Singapore, according to a University of Oxford–led study published in People and Nature.

science.title: Seismic imaging reveals double slab tearing at a subduction–collision transition
science.summary: An international research team has used seismic imaging to identify two slab tears beneath the Zagros–Makran transition zone located in southeastern Iran near the Strait of Hormuz. The findings suggest that the tears formed through distinct geodynamic mechanisms and may have influenced regional tectonic deformation and magmatic activity.

science.title: Watching others pays off: Attentive macaques benefit from observing their group mates interacting
science.summary: Monkeys constantly observe and evaluate their social environment. It stands to reason that the social and mental abilities required to do so were favored by evolution. After all, these abilities should influence how an animal interacts with its conspecifics and, as a result, what social position it can attain within the group's hierarchy. Researchers from the DPZ and the University of Göttingen have now investigated whether this widely held assumption is correct by studying 46 wild male Assamese macaques in Thailand. The paper is published in the journal Current Biology.

science.title: Promising new biomarkers to diagnose feline chronic kidney disease
science.summary: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is common in cats but often goes undiagnosed until it's at a late stage. Thanks to a recent study published in the Journal of Proteome Research, researchers have new leads to determine how feline CKD develops. The paper reports collections of potential protein biomarkers in urine that could help veterinarians detect different stages of the disease and develop more targeted and effective treatments for this irreversible ailment.

science.title: Interdisciplinarity on the curriculum—teachers hold different views on what students should learn
science.summary: The climate transition, energy supply and technological development are just some examples of areas where knowledge from several disciplines needs to come together to find relevant solutions. Engineering students are therefore often given the opportunity to work on interdisciplinary projects. But the term "interdisciplinary" encompasses widely differing ideas about what the teaching should involve and what students are actually expected to learn. This is shown by a study in which researchers interviewed 18 teachers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, Aalto University in Finland and Aalborg University in Denmark. The paper is published in the Journal of Engineering Education.

science.title: Chirality of 'trions' illuminates new paths for quantum optics
science.summary: Scientists from Tokyo Metropolitan University have discovered that charged states made of two electrons and a positively charged hole (or vice versa) on atomically thin rolls of carbon atoms have a structure-derived "handedness" in how they interact with light. While electron-hole pairs, or "excitons," were known to keep the chirality of the underlying nanotube, the team showed that adding a charge to create "trions" does not change this property.

science.title: How bacteria build the molecular bushing of the flagellar motor
science.summary: The bacterial flagellum is a motility organelle that enables bacteria to swim and is composed of more than 30 different proteins. Researchers have long sought to understand how this complex nanomachine self-assembles from many parts in the correct order and at the correct positions. In a study published in Communications Biology, a research team at the University of Osaka revealed the mechanism by which the flagellar motor assembles its bushing around the drive shaft.

science.title: Ancient underwater canyons reveal clues to the world's oldest animal life
science.summary: Geologists have uncovered new evidence that dramatic sea-level changes carved giant underwater canyons in South Australia's Flinders Ranges hundreds of millions of years ago, helping to create conditions that preserved some of the earliest complex life on Earth. The findings, led by Adelaide University, shed new light on the environmental changes that accompanied the rise of the mysterious Ediacaran biota.

science.title: Removing too much crop waste for bioenergy could come at a cost to biodiversity, study finds
science.summary: Crop residues—the stems, leaves and husks left behind after harvesting cereals—could provide an important source of renewable energy for Europe, but research led by the University of Surrey suggests that removing too much from fields could come at a cost to biodiversity.

science.title: The migration that remade Africa
science.summary: It's not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between A.D. 1000 and 1700—were masters.

science.title: A hummingbird's brilliant magenta feathers depend on a hidden middle layer
science.summary: The brilliant magenta feathers on the head and throat of a male Anna's hummingbird present an optical puzzle. Magenta cannot be produced by a single wavelength of light. Instead, the feathers reflect a mixture of red and blue. Scientists understood the strong red reflection, but the weaker blue component was harder to explain.

science.title: CT scanning the centuries-old head of Jeremy Bentham
science.summary: Cutting-edge medical imaging techniques have revealed that Jeremy Bentham, the Georgian philosopher and reformer, suffered from chronic toothache and a jaw riddled with arthritis.

science.title: Sell-side analysts fail to adequately adjust stock forecasts after Fed meetings
science.summary: When the U.S. Federal Reserve announces a change in its interest rate, consumers expect shifts in borrowing costs elsewhere and potential price adjustments for things like housing and some consumer goods. New research, however, shows that stock market analysts generally give a collective "meh" around the time of Fed meetings when it comes to forecasting how much stocks will trade for in the future, called a price target.

science.title: A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid
science.summary: Scientists have observed a bizarre quantum state of matter that combines the structure of a crystal with the frictionless flow of a liquid, all at room temperature. The breakthrough overturns a major practical limitation of exotic quantum experiments and could help bring powerful new light-based computing and sensing technologies closer to reality.

science.title: Crystals hint at a volcano's ability to erupt
science.summary: University of Queensland researchers have shown tiny crystals are a window to activity inside volcanoes and could provide clues to when they might erupt.

science.title: NASA reveals bold new plan to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028
science.summary: NASA has revealed an accelerated plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing competing lunar landers and a crucial orbital test scheduled for 2027. Faster rocket preparations, new lightweight spacesuits, and redesigned missions could help pave the way for a permanent lunar presence and future human exploration of Mars.

environment.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
environment.summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

environment.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
environment.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

environment.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
environment.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

environment.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.

environment.title: “Crawzilla” was huge. Then scientists found an even bigger crayfish
environment.summary: A nationwide search for giant crayfish uncovered a record-breaking Tennessee specimen and a surprising mystery about how big these freshwater creatures can grow. Scientists found that North American crayfish seem to hit a biological size limit, possibly because of their muscles or protective shells.

mix_items.title: Two nearby rocky worlds could offer alien astronomers views of planets appearing to reverse course
mix_items.summary: Aliens have long been a staple of science fiction. Yet the possibility of intelligent life beyond Earth is more than a matter of imagination—it is also a subject of serious scientific inquiry. Professor Woong-bae Zee of Sejong University's School of Liberal Studies has recently published an astronomy paper that places the word "alien" front and center.

mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.summary: „Visul meu este să ajung doctor pediatru și să pot ajuta mult copiii”, spune Gabriela, o adolescentă în vârstă de... Articolul Gabriela, adolescenta care visează să devină medic pediatru apare prima dată în World Vision România .

mix_items.title: The fastest levitated spinning magnet ever made might help physicists search for dark matter
mix_items.summary: Tiny levitated magnets are able to avoid contact friction, making them useful for detecting extremely weak forces and magnetic fields and acting as ultralow-noise quantum sensors and precision measurement tools. Combining levitation with extreme cold further reduces unwanted motion that can make faint signals hard to detect.

mix_items.summary: Peste 500 de copii au participat la activități de educație nonformală și wellbeing derulate de Fundația Inocenți cu sprijinul Pepco România. The post Sute de copii sprijiniți prin educație nonformală de Inocenți și Pepco appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Satellite monitoring of the world's oceans is being restricted by legal barriers, study suggests
mix_items.summary: Satellite technology can increasingly track vessels across the world's oceans and has the ability to detect industrial fishing inside marine protected areas (MPAs). But new research has suggested that regulations governing these often vulnerable parts of our planet could be preventing global authorities from turning satellite detection into effective enforcement.

mix_items.title: Could the way we walk give clues about our mental health?
mix_items.summary: Experts in kinesiology and sport sciences and psychology from the University of Miami are collaborating on research to find out whether the way people walk could give clues about their mental health. The two researchers are exploring this question through a project called MindStep, where participants answer survey questions about their mental health and then complete different intellectual tasks while walking, as specialized cameras record and measure their walking patterns.

mix_items.title: Repeated racism linked to depression and suicidal thoughts in Colorado teens
mix_items.summary: Knowing that multiple studies provide strong evidence that links racism to poor mental health, researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz wanted to know what types of racist incidents young people are experiencing in schools and if repeated events were more harmful to their mental health.

mix_items.title: The art of good conversation may involve a little pink noise
mix_items.summary: Most of us like a good old chat with friends, colleagues, neighbors or acquaintances. But what can turn a really good chat into a great one? Sure, conversation topics matter, but scientists have found underlying patterns that may explain our best interactions.

mix_items.title: Prehistoric whale reveals extreme skull asymmetry
mix_items.summary: Sperm whales and pygmy sperm whales are known among mammals for their unusually shaped heads. Unlike most vertebrates, which are bilaterally symmetrical, toothed whales have asymmetrical skulls that accommodate highly specialized organs used for echolocation and sound production.

mix_items.title: Scientists turn protein-making errors in cancer cells into a targeted kill switch
mix_items.summary: Like every other cell in the human body, cancer cells also produce their own share of proteins for survival. During this production process, cells often encounter a glitch called ribosomal frameshifting. This exceptionally rare event occurs roughly once in every 100,000 translation events, when the ribosome, while reading genetic instructions to make a protein, shifts its reading position. A recent Nature study investigated whether this protein-building glitch in cancer cells can be turned into a targeted cancer therapy.

mix_items.title: Smart use of trees and crops brings best yield
mix_items.summary: Cultivating crops—such as wheat, barley and rye—alongside rows of trees is a system of agroforestry that is known as "alley-cropping." It serves many functions: in addition to enhancing ecosystems and biodiversity, it can also counteract the negative effects of growing crops in treeless open land. The advantages of alley-cropping come from the interaction between trees and crops, resulting in improved soil quality, reduced wind erosion, enhanced nutrient cycling, and climate change mitigation through increased carbon capture.

mix_items.title: The brain's 'dimmer switch' could help explain why attention drifts
mix_items.summary: McGill researchers have discovered that serotonin, a brain chemical best known for its role in mood and mental health, also helps regulate attention. "Our findings suggest serotonin-producing neurons deep in the midbrain act like a dimmer switch on attention," said Arjun Krishnaswamy, associate professor in the Department of Physiology, who co-led the study with associate professor Erik Cook. The findings were published in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: 'Nice' by any other name means essentially the same thing
mix_items.summary: Is any good deed truly selfless—and does it matter?

mix_items.title: Cells 'sense' physical forces to seal tissues and protect organs
mix_items.summary: Northwestern Medicine scientists have uncovered a molecular mechanism that enables cells to protect organs from leaks, infection and inflammation, according to a study published in the Journal of Cell Biology. The findings of the study add to scientific understanding of how epithelial cells maintain protective barriers, said senior author Cara J. Gottardi, professor of medicine in the Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care and of cell and developmental biology.

mix_items.title: Organizations call for rapid, team-based endovascular hemorrhage control in trauma care
mix_items.summary: The American College of Surgeons (ACS) Committee on Trauma and the Society of Interventional Radiology (SIR) have issued a joint position statement reaffirming the role of interventional radiologists on multidisciplinary trauma teams and the importance of establishing reliable systems for rapid endovascular hemorrhage control in trauma situations.

mix_items.title: Why demand persists for the horn of a once near-extinct antelope
mix_items.summary: Family traditions, misconceptions about where it comes from, and a belief that remedies sold in shops are government-approved help explain continued demand for saiga antelope horn in Singapore, according to a University of Oxford–led study published in People and Nature.

mix_items.title: Seismic imaging reveals double slab tearing at a subduction–collision transition
mix_items.summary: An international research team has used seismic imaging to identify two slab tears beneath the Zagros–Makran transition zone located in southeastern Iran near the Strait of Hormuz. The findings suggest that the tears formed through distinct geodynamic mechanisms and may have influenced regional tectonic deformation and magmatic activity.

mix_items.title: AI assesses what really matters to people in health care—well-being
mix_items.summary: Artificial intelligence is helping to analyze and improve health care systems—from waiting times to treatment outcomes and costs. However, some of the most important aspects of care remain harder to measure—such as whether people feel heard, understood and genuinely cared for.

mix_items.title: Watching others pays off: Attentive macaques benefit from observing their group mates interacting
mix_items.summary: Monkeys constantly observe and evaluate their social environment. It stands to reason that the social and mental abilities required to do so were favored by evolution. After all, these abilities should influence how an animal interacts with its conspecifics and, as a result, what social position it can attain within the group's hierarchy. Researchers from the DPZ and the University of Göttingen have now investigated whether this widely held assumption is correct by studying 46 wild male Assamese macaques in Thailand. The paper is published in the journal Current Biology.

mix_items.title: Early trial results suggest potential new treatment for stiff person syndrome
mix_items.summary: A multicenter clinical trial evaluating chimeric antigen receptor-T cell therapy (CAR-T cell therapy) for stiff person syndrome (SPS), a rare autoimmune neurologic disorder, has produced promising early results.

mix_items.title: US youths see nearly 4,000 food marketing messages on digital media each year
mix_items.summary: U.S. children and adolescents see thousands of food marketing messages on digital media platforms each year, according to new research published in JAMA Pediatrics. And 92% of the marketed food and beverage products are considered unhealthy.

mix_items.title: Promising new biomarkers to diagnose feline chronic kidney disease
mix_items.summary: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is common in cats but often goes undiagnosed until it's at a late stage. Thanks to a recent study published in the Journal of Proteome Research, researchers have new leads to determine how feline CKD develops. The paper reports collections of potential protein biomarkers in urine that could help veterinarians detect different stages of the disease and develop more targeted and effective treatments for this irreversible ailment.

mix_items.title: It takes a neighborhood to keep kids active
mix_items.summary: Getting youngsters to go outside and play doesn't just rely on family support, but also on a neighborhood coming together to create a good environment, University of Alberta research shows.

mix_items.title: Interdisciplinarity on the curriculum—teachers hold different views on what students should learn
mix_items.summary: The climate transition, energy supply and technological development are just some examples of areas where knowledge from several disciplines needs to come together to find relevant solutions. Engineering students are therefore often given the opportunity to work on interdisciplinary projects. But the term "interdisciplinary" encompasses widely differing ideas about what the teaching should involve and what students are actually expected to learn. This is shown by a study in which researchers interviewed 18 teachers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, Aalto University in Finland and Aalborg University in Denmark. The paper is published in the Journal of Engineering Education.

mix_items.title: Chirality of 'trions' illuminates new paths for quantum optics
mix_items.summary: Scientists from Tokyo Metropolitan University have discovered that charged states made of two electrons and a positively charged hole (or vice versa) on atomically thin rolls of carbon atoms have a structure-derived "handedness" in how they interact with light. While electron-hole pairs, or "excitons," were known to keep the chirality of the underlying nanotube, the team showed that adding a charge to create "trions" does not change this property.

mix_items.title: Two-year study will examine how gender-affirming hormone therapy affects energy use and blood vessel function
mix_items.summary: The research team at the LeiCeM Cluster of Excellence is preparing a new study. It builds on the first phase of the Hormones and Health study (HHS), in which researchers from the Helmholtz Institute for Metabolic, Obesity and Vascular Research (HI-MAG), Leipzig University and the University of Leipzig Medical Center followed trans people undergoing gender-affirming hormone therapy. The second cohort will be studied over a period of two years, with the study expected to begin in early 2027.

mix_items.title: How bacteria build the molecular bushing of the flagellar motor
mix_items.summary: The bacterial flagellum is a motility organelle that enables bacteria to swim and is composed of more than 30 different proteins. Researchers have long sought to understand how this complex nanomachine self-assembles from many parts in the correct order and at the correct positions. In a study published in Communications Biology, a research team at the University of Osaka revealed the mechanism by which the flagellar motor assembles its bushing around the drive shaft.

mix_items.title: Study challenges long-held fears about overactive bladder drugs and dementia
mix_items.summary: New research published in JAMA Network Open finds anticholinergic medications, commonly prescribed for overactive bladder (OAB), may not increase dementia risk after all compared to beta-3 agonists, the newer drug class that has been presumed to be safer for the brain.

mix_items.title: Ancient underwater canyons reveal clues to the world's oldest animal life
mix_items.summary: Geologists have uncovered new evidence that dramatic sea-level changes carved giant underwater canyons in South Australia's Flinders Ranges hundreds of millions of years ago, helping to create conditions that preserved some of the earliest complex life on Earth. The findings, led by Adelaide University, shed new light on the environmental changes that accompanied the rise of the mysterious Ediacaran biota.

mix_items.title: Removing too much crop waste for bioenergy could come at a cost to biodiversity, study finds
mix_items.summary: Crop residues—the stems, leaves and husks left behind after harvesting cereals—could provide an important source of renewable energy for Europe, but research led by the University of Surrey suggests that removing too much from fields could come at a cost to biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Why obesity affects males and females differently
mix_items.summary: University of California, Riverside, scientists have an explanation for why males and females respond differently to obesity. They report in PNAS Nexus that certain immune cell populations in fat tissue may protect against obesity-related inflammation while others may contribute to harmful metabolic changes. They found these immune cells, called eosinophils and traditionally associated with asthma and allergies, behave differently in males and females.

mix_items.title: Your brain may map emotional concepts onto a hexagonal grid, new study suggests
mix_items.summary: Everyday life throws a whole range of emotional experiences our way, from exciting and relaxing moments to tense or gloomy encounters. Each experience is shaped by what's present around us in the moment, the sensations our body is experiencing and our past experiences. This entire scene is set by the brain, which draws on these experiences of the past, organizing the information it gathers into mental maps that help us predict what might happen and respond appropriately to different situations.

mix_items.title: The migration that remade Africa
mix_items.summary: It's not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between A.D. 1000 and 1700—were masters.

mix_items.title: In phase 2 trial, novel therapy significantly reduced triglyceride levels
mix_items.summary: A phase 2b clinical trial led by Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute researchers shows that a monoclonal antibody therapy called MAR001 can significantly reduce triglyceride levels within 12 weeks for patients with high triglyceride levels. Their results are published in the New England Journal of Medicine and were presented simultaneously at the American Heart Association's annual meeting.

mix_items.title: Childhood cancers may spread by 'shape-shifting' rather than mutating
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of East Anglia (UK) have proposed an explanation for why some childhood tumors spread aggressively around the body despite having relatively few genetic faults. For years, experts believed cancers become more dangerous by accumulating genetic mutations that allow them to invade new tissues and evade treatment. But a new paper shows how childhood cancers may not always need extra mutations to spread.

mix_items.title: ‘Digital advances are reshaping nature conservation’ say experts
mix_items.summary: Technology and the rapid advance of AI are opening up new possibilities in the race to save nature, according to a report The post ‘Digital advances are reshaping nature conservation’ say experts appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: Magnetic fields can revive intracellular transport in ALS
mix_items.summary: A study led by cell biologist Dr. Arun Pal at the HZDR, in collaboration with research partners in Dresden and Rostock, has found that electromagnetic alternating fields can partially reverse key pathological changes in human nerve cells. The finding has been published in the journal Cells.

mix_items.title: Cleaner bedroom air may help manage blood sugar in prediabetes
mix_items.summary: Using portable filters to reduce exposure to air pollution during sleep may stabilize the large spikes in blood sugar experienced by people with prediabetes, a condition in which sugar (glucose) levels are higher than normal, a new study shows.

mix_items.title: Concussion study upends understanding of what makes head impacts dangerous
mix_items.summary: Concussions—essentially mild traumatic brain injuries—are among the most common injuries sustained on athletic fields. In the U.S., an estimated 3.8 million sports-related concussions occur every year. But new research by Stanford Medicine scientists and collaborators suggests that the prevailing understanding of the forces that lead to concussion may be missing the mark.

mix_items.title: A hummingbird's brilliant magenta feathers depend on a hidden middle layer
mix_items.summary: The brilliant magenta feathers on the head and throat of a male Anna's hummingbird present an optical puzzle. Magenta cannot be produced by a single wavelength of light. Instead, the feathers reflect a mixture of red and blue. Scientists understood the strong red reflection, but the weaker blue component was harder to explain.

mix_items.title: CT scanning the centuries-old head of Jeremy Bentham
mix_items.summary: Cutting-edge medical imaging techniques have revealed that Jeremy Bentham, the Georgian philosopher and reformer, suffered from chronic toothache and a jaw riddled with arthritis.

mix_items.title: Sell-side analysts fail to adequately adjust stock forecasts after Fed meetings
mix_items.summary: When the U.S. Federal Reserve announces a change in its interest rate, consumers expect shifts in borrowing costs elsewhere and potential price adjustments for things like housing and some consumer goods. New research, however, shows that stock market analysts generally give a collective "meh" around the time of Fed meetings when it comes to forecasting how much stocks will trade for in the future, called a price target.

mix_items.title: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that pantethine, a readily available vitamin B5 derivative, can calm overactive immune cells and may help fight psoriasis. The supplement prevented psoriasis in mice and showed promising results in a small human trial, revealing an unexpected connection between cholesterol and autoimmune inflammation.

mix_items.title: A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid
mix_items.summary: Scientists have observed a bizarre quantum state of matter that combines the structure of a crystal with the frictionless flow of a liquid, all at room temperature. The breakthrough overturns a major practical limitation of exotic quantum experiments and could help bring powerful new light-based computing and sensing technologies closer to reality.

mix_items.title: A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study from UCLA suggests that a naturally occurring molecule could help breast cancer survivors overcome the frustrating brain fog and exhaustion that can linger long after treatment ends. Researchers found that women taking an oxaloacetate supplement for eight weeks experienced substantial improvements in memory, concentration, mental clarity, and fatigue.

mix_items.title: Crystals hint at a volcano's ability to erupt
mix_items.summary: University of Queensland researchers have shown tiny crystals are a window to activity inside volcanoes and could provide clues to when they might erupt.

mix_items.title: AI predicts PTSD risk based on stories about what brought patients to the emergency room
mix_items.summary: An AI tool can analyze patients' narratives about injuries that sent them to the emergency room to predict who will later develop posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a new study found.

mix_items.title: Could a plant metabolite act as a natural sunscreen to help prevent skin cancer?
mix_items.summary: Research in Photochemistry and Photobiology indicates that a plant metabolite that can block the effects of ultraviolet (UV) light has promising potential as a natural sunscreen when applied to human skin.

mix_items.title: NASA reveals bold new plan to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028
mix_items.summary: NASA has revealed an accelerated plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing competing lunar landers and a crucial orbital test scheduled for 2027. Faster rocket preparations, new lightweight spacesuits, and redesigned missions could help pave the way for a permanent lunar presence and future human exploration of Mars.

mix_items.title: Cancer clinical trial participants reimbursed a median $2,128 for nonmedical expenses
mix_items.summary: New research reveals that participating in cancer clinical trials can cause financial burdens that are shaped by both socioeconomic and logistical factors. The analysis published by Wiley online in CANCER, indicates the need for better reimbursement programs to improve equitable access to, and retention in, cancer clinical trials.

mix_items.title: Amazon mapping shows cacao expansion without deforestation in Brazil
mix_items.summary: While West Africa clears rainforest for chocolate, Brazilian farmers are reviving degraded pastures.

mix_items.title: Money laundering complaints target JBS, Barclays over profits linked to illegal deforestation
mix_items.summary: A coalition of legal and environmental groups has filed money laundering complaints against JBS, the world’s largest meat processor, and 12 financial institutions, investors and advisers, including the U.K. bank Barclays. The complaints allegedly tie JBS profits to illegal deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon. The Transnational Legal Coalition filed 14 complaints with prosecutors and financial […]

mix_items.title: 3M agrees to pay more than $7 billion to settle ‘forever chemical’ groundwater contamination claims
mix_items.summary: Chemical manufacturer 3M will pay up to $7.35 billion to settle lawsuits by people who say they were sickened by groundwater contamination from compounds used in firefighting foam and other consumer products. The St. Paul, Minnesota-based company announced the settlement Tuesday. It will pay the money over nine years to as many as 120,000 people […]

mix_items.title: How Ghana’s new license to sell sustainable timber improves institutions & cooperation (analysis)
mix_items.summary: When Ghana began its Voluntary Partnership Agreement (VPA) process with the European Union, the attraction was clear. Europe is an important market for Ghanaian timber, international expectations around its legality were changing, and the VPA offered both market access and support for strengthening national forest governance. After a 16-year journey, last year Ghana became the […]

mix_items.title: What went right this week: the good news that matters
mix_items.summary: Nature was restored at ‘unprecedented scale’, Barbados halted HIV transmission in babies, and a fuel revolution picked up speed, plus more The post What went right this week: the good news that matters appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
mix_items.summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

mix_items.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
mix_items.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
mix_items.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.

mix_items.title: “Crawzilla” was huge. Then scientists found an even bigger crayfish
mix_items.summary: A nationwide search for giant crayfish uncovered a record-breaking Tennessee specimen and a surprising mystery about how big these freshwater creatures can grow. Scientists found that North American crayfish seem to hit a biological size limit, possibly because of their muscles or protective shells.
